title: CoMind: Towards Community-Driven Agents for Machine Learning Engineering
one_liner: CoMind treats machine-learning engineering as a community problem rather than a single-agent problem, so several agents explore candidate solutions in parallel and exchange externally sourced knowledge before deciding what to implement next.
lead: Most machine-learning engineering agents work in isolation. They read a problem statement, try a pipeline, and improve it from their own earlier attempts, so the search stays limited to what one trajectory discovers because no parallel branch tests a competing design at the same time. Human competitors in research settings such as Kaggle do more than that. They read discussions, compare ideas, adapt community findings, and test several solution branches at once. CoMind brings that pattern into an agent system. It uses a multi-agent loop with parallel exploration and a community-aware evaluation setup, so the agent can search broader idea space while still implementing and validating concrete solutions.

problem.h2: A lone agent explores too narrowly for open-ended ML engineering
paras: Machine-learning engineering tasks such as Kaggle competitions are not single-step question answering problems. They require data inspection, feature design, model choice, validation strategy, and repeated error analysis. A single agent that follows one solution path at a time can get trapped in a narrow region of the search space, especially when the first promising idea is not the best one.

Human competitors reduce that risk by using community signals. They inspect public discussions, borrow useful diagnostics, and compare several candidate approaches before committing more compute. Existing agents usually skip that external collective process. As a result, they may implement one coherent pipeline but miss stronger ideas already visible in the broader research conversation.

callout.html: CoMind evaluates agents in a live community setting and uses multiple collaborating agents that explore several solution branches while incorporating outside knowledge from that setting.

steps.b: Set up a live-style engineering task
steps.text: Use the MLE-Live framework so the agent must work in a simulated research community rather than a sealed benchmark.
Assign different agents or roles to pursue different solution ideas in parallel.
Read external hints, earlier findings, and public discussion signals when they are useful.
Run code, evaluate validation results, and compare branches quantitatively.

steps.text: Select or combine the strongest components into the final solution.

paras: CoMind changes the unit of problem solving from one isolated agent trajectory to a coordinated search process. The important change is not just that there are many agents, but that they explore in parallel, exchange findings, and incorporate community knowledge before narrowing down to a final implementation.
object.object: the search procedure for ML engineering solutions

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: exploratory coverage with validation pressure
hidden.name: search coverage under validation
paras: The central quantity is how much of the useful solution space the system explores before it spends too much time polishing the wrong branch. Breadth alone is not enough, because unlimited branching wastes compute. Depth alone is not enough, because one branch can miss the highest-scoring approach entirely.

CoMind balances those needs by running several branches in parallel and then using measured outcomes to decide which branches deserve more resources. Community knowledge widens the candidate set, while local implementation and validation prevent the system from accepting untested suggestions at face value.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark parts of the search that contribute useful coverage while still being tied to measured validation outcomes.

reads.html: The system should explore several serious solution ideas, but it should keep spending effort only on the branches that validation says are worth it.
CoMind uses iterative parallel exploration to trade off exploratory breadth and implementation depth within the MLE-Live community setting.

paras: Open-ended ML engineering is a search problem over pipelines, not a direct mapping from prompt to answer. There are choices about preprocessing, validation, model family, ensembling, and post-processing, and these choices interact. A single trajectory can easily overfit early evidence. Parallel exploration reduces that risk because several incompatible ideas can be tested at once rather than sequentially after one branch has already consumed most of the budget.

Community knowledge expands the proposal set. Public discussions or earlier competition findings often reveal failure modes such as leakage, target imbalance, or feature drift. An isolated agent may rediscover these issues late or miss them entirely. A community-driven agent can import those hypotheses earlier, then test them directly in code rather than copying them blindly.

Validation pressure is the mechanism that keeps the system grounded. Parallel branches are useful only if weak branches are pruned and strong branches are promoted based on observed leaderboard or validation evidence. CoMind therefore benefits from both social input and experimental discipline: community signals propose where to search, and branch-level evaluation decides what survives.

stages.s: Competition task plus access to community signals
Import useful outside hints into selected branches
Implement and validate branches in parallel
Prune weak branches and merge strong ideas

math.words: Allocate more resources to branches whose measured score is high after accounting for branch cost, and reduce effort on branches whose score gain does not justify more work.
symbols: how much additional effort branch b receives in the next round
the estimated usefulness of continuing branch b based on current evidence

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose Branch A is a feature-engineering pipeline and Branch B is a new model family.
Branch A improves validation by 0.02 with little extra compute. Branch B improves validation by 0.01 but requires a long retraining run.
If both branches started with equal budget, the next round should send more effort to Branch A because its measured gain per unit cost is higher.
If a community hint later suggests that Branch B is likely to combine well with ensembling, Branch B can receive renewed budget and be tested again.

math.note: The exact scoring rule can vary, but the principle is to combine outside hints with measured branch outcomes rather than following one path by default.

items.html: If the system keeps too many weak branches alive, implementation effort is spread thinly and none of the strong ideas is developed far enough to matter.
Public hints may reflect local leaderboard effects or mistaken diagnoses, so importing them without validation can send the system toward brittle or irrelevant solutions.
If branches are evaluated with inconsistent validation splits or different compute budgets, the promotion rule can favor the wrong branch for procedural reasons rather than real quality.
The method works best when branch count stays limited, branch evaluation is consistent, and outside suggestions are treated as hypotheses to test rather than as facts to trust automatically.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Create a small ML engineering benchmark with several tabular prediction tasks, a discussion board containing both useful and noisy hints, and a tool interface for training, validation, and feature inspection. Compare one isolated agent against a multi-agent system that can explore several branches in parallel and read the discussion board.

The demo should log how many distinct branches were tested, which outside hints were adopted, which branches were pruned, and the final held-out score. The method's key claim is supported if the multi-agent system reaches stronger final pipelines because it searched more broadly but still used measured validation to decide what to keep.
demo.closing: A convincing result shows that community-aware parallel search finds stronger pipelines than an isolated single-trajectory agent under the same overall budget, because several branches can test incompatible ideas in parallel and validation can keep only the ones that actually improve score.
